rounds.question: What did Jacques de Meulles improvise to pay troops in New France when coins ran short in 1685?
rounds.truth: Playing cards, cut to different shapes and signed with their monetary values on the backs.

rounds.question: Why could two copies of the same early Bible edition disagree even though neither reader had altered a word?
rounds.truth: Corrections were made while the press kept working, so uncorrected sheets could be mixed with corrected ones in finished copies.

rounds.question: How can traces of Egyptian blue reveal themselves even when their colour is hard to see?
rounds.truth: They emit near-infrared light when illuminated, allowing specialised imaging to map the pigment.

rounds.question: What did Shackleton’s men call “the thief” during their 1916 voyage in the James Caird?
rounds.truth: A narrow metal dipper used to measure out their drinking water.

rounds.question: What did Special Operations Executive agents tie over their boots before wading ashore in the Pacific theatre?
rounds.truth: Rubber overshoes cast as bare human feet, so their tracks would read as a local's rather than a soldier's.

rounds.question: Why can Actaea pachypoda use birds as delivery agents even though its berries are dangerously toxic to people?
rounds.truth: Many birds are immune to the berries' toxic effects and spread the seeds after eating them.
